title: New Patient Prescribing
description: Learn how medicine requests are assessed for new patients, including the need for records, monitoring or further clinical review.
headings: Prescribing starts with a safe clinical review.
How to prepare for your appointment
text: Patient Information New Patient Prescribing Policy A clear guide to how medicine requests are reviewed when you are new to the practice. For new patients Prescribing starts with a safe clinical review. We welcome new patients, including people who already take regular medicines. A prescription is not automatic, however. Your doctor must be satisfied that prescribing is safe, clinically appropriate and supported by enough information about your health and current treatment. Prescribing restrictions for new patients Controlled, dependence-forming and high-risk medicines. These may not be prescribed at a first appointment without adequate verification, clinical assessment and any monitoring the doctor considers necessary. Existing long-term medicines. Your doctor may need previous records, specialist letters, recent test results or confirmation from your usual prescriber or pharmacy before continuing a medicine. Medicines requiring ongoing monitoring. A consultation, examination, pathology, other testing or specialist review may be required before a prescription can be issued. Requests that are not clinically appropriate. A doctor may decline, defer or recommend a different treatment pathway when prescribing would not be safe or appropriate. How to prepare for your appointment Bring an up-to-date medication list and, if useful, the medicine packaging. Bring relevant specialist letters, recent results or a health summary if you have them. Tell reception if the appointment relates to a medicine that may require a longer review. Book before your medicine supply runs out so there is time to review records or arrange follow-up if needed. Clinical judgement comes first. Reception can help with appointment arrangements, but only a qualified prescriber can decide whether a medicine should be prescribed, continued, changed or stopped. Patient questions Frequently Asked Questions Will I automatically receive my regular medicines at my first appointment? No. Prescribing is a clinical decision. Your doctor may need to confirm your medical history, current medicines, monitoring and previous records before deciding whether a prescription is appropriate. What if I take a controlled or dependence-forming medicine? New patients should not assume controlled, dependence-forming or other high-risk medicines will be prescribed at a first visit. The doctor may require records, additional assessment, monitoring or advice from your usual prescriber or specialist. What should I bring if I need a medication review? Bring an up-to-date medication list, medicine packaging if useful, relevant specialist letters and details of your usual prescriber or pharmacy. What if I am running out of medicine? Book early rather than waiting until your supply has run out. If you are concerned about missing a medicine or possible withdrawal, contact reception for advice about the most appropriate care pathway. For a medical emergency, call 000. title: Repeat Scripts
description: Prescription renewals are part of clinical care and may require an appointment so your medication can be reviewed safely.
text: Patient Information Repeat Scripts Prescription renewals are part of clinical care and may require an appointment so your medication can be reviewed safely. Information for patients of Woolloongabba Medical Centre in Brisbane’s inner south. Renewing a prescription Our current policy requires a consultation with a doctor for further prescriptions. This allows the prescriber to confirm that the medicine remains appropriate and that any monitoring or follow-up is up to date. Some repeat prescriptions for regular medication may be suitable for a brief consultation, while other prescription requests may require a standard or longer appointment. Electronic prescriptions An electronic prescription is a digital alternative to a paper prescription. If your prescriber offers an eScript and it is appropriate for your medicine, a secure token can be sent by SMS or email and presented to a pharmacy for dispensing. If a prescription has repeats, the pharmacy can issue a new token after each dispensing. If you lose an original token, contact the prescriber; for a repeat token, contact the pharmacy that issued it. Electronic prescriptions — Australian Digital Health Agency Medication safety A prescription may not be renewed automatically. Your doctor may need to review your symptoms, dose, side effects, interactions, monitoring tests or the length of time you have been taking the medicine before prescribing again. Choosing the right appointment A repeat prescription for regular medication may be suitable for a brief appointment in some circumstances. A medication request that needs discussion may require a standard or longer consultation. Your doctor will advise if more time is needed for clinical review. Prescription questions Do I need a consultation for a repeat prescription? Our policy requires a consultation with a doctor for further prescriptions so the prescriber can confirm that the medicine remains appropriate. Can a repeat prescription be a brief appointment? Some repeat prescriptions for regular medication may be suitable for a brief consultation, while other requests may require a standard or longer review. Book an appointment → Can an electronic prescription be sent to my phone? Where clinically appropriate and supported by the prescriber, an electronic prescription token can be sent by SMS or email and presented to a participating pharmacy.
